pulls.title: Initial content: SLH-DSA-FEW (SP 800-230) for X.509
pulls.author: fluppe2
pulls.body:
First full draft text, merging two sources:

- RFC 9909 (FelixKnopp/x509-slhdsa@b3b216f) as the base
- Felix's draft on branch `add-slh-dsa-24-parameter-sets` (FelixKnopp/x509-slhdsa@811cd19)

## Contents
- Pure and HashSLH-DSA-FEW OIDs (`TBD1`–`TBD12`, to be assigned by NIST), in SP 800-230 order
- "Use in X.509" section referring to RFC 9909 Sections 4–7
- Operational and security considerations for the 2^24 signature limit: pointer to SP 800-230 Section 3, CA/CRL/OCSP; keys that sign on demand (TLS, OCSP) are not suited for SLH-DSA-FEW and MUST NOT use it unless the limit can be guaranteed (in line with SP 800-230 §3)
- Complete ASN.1 module (`asn1/X509-SLHDSA-FEW-2026.asn`) including `SignatureAlgorithms`, `SMimeCaps`, `PublicKeyAlgorithms`; module OID requested in the SMI PKIX module registry
- Authors: Kaveh Bashiri, Felix Knopp, Stavros Kousidis
- `CODEOWNERS` for `@spec-workbench/slhdsa-fewsigs-editors`, placeholder `examples/`

## Changes compared to Felix's branch, please review
- Removed the claim that security "does not degrade gradually" beyond the limit; replaced it with "no longer guaranteed" plus an editor's note. Please check against KP22 / SP 800-230.
- Reworded "signatures generated beyond the limit are indistinguishable from valid ones" to refer to forgeries.
- Fixed the ASN.1 module (`# Todo` line, module OID arc, missing `SignatureAlgorithms`/`SMimeCaps` sets, set name `PublicKeyAlgorithms`).
- IANA: standard request in "SMI Security for PKIX Module Identifier" instead of "to be determined".

## Open issues (editor's notes in the draft)
- OIDs from NIST CSOR
- Re-check against the final SP 800-230
- HashSLH-DSA-FEW: needed? NIST OIDs?
- CMS in this document or a separate one?

Builds cleanly; `make idnits` shows no errors (remaining warnings: RFC 5912 downref, which is in the downref registry, and `<CODE BEGINS>`, both as in RFC 9909).

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

comments.author: fluppe2
comments.body:
Thanks, @BashiriK  and @FelixKnopp. I took your suggestions in the commit I just pushed, with a few corrections:

- SP 800-230 has no Operational or Security Considerations sections. Its requirements are in Section 3, “Usage and Security Requirements”, so both places now refer to that section.
- Applying the suggestions on lines 326–329 and 330–348 together would have cut a sentence short (“… parameter set MUST NOT” followed by “If the evaluation …”). The opening of the Security Considerations is now one paragraph. It points to RFC 9909 and SP 800-230 Section 3, and states the 2^24 MUST NOT as replacing the 2^64.
- As you suggested, the evaluation list is gone. The remaining MUST NOT refers to the evaluation required by SP 800-230 Section 3.
- I kept the paragraph saying that a relying party cannot detect an exceeded limit. That point is specific to X.509 and isn’t in SP 800-230.
- In the Operational Considerations, the lowercase “must not” sentence is replaced by a pointer to Section 3, so we don’t state the requirement once without and once with BCP 14 keywords.

I’ll resolve your suggestion threads. If this works for you, please (both) approve and I’ll merge.

comments.body: The existing `Update Generated Files` workflow explicitly regenerates `.github/CODEOWNERS` and removes customizations. Its next manual run will therefore overwrite this team rule and remove the intended all-files editor ownership. Please make the team rule persist through that workflow, or exclude this file from regeneration.

A certificate's expiration date does not stop its private key from signing, and the key may also have been used before issuance or under another certificate. Base any time bound on the key's remaining signature budget and maximum aggregate signing rate, and enforce retirement of every copy at the deadline.

The PR description says this should state that the claimed security is “no longer guaranteed,” but this paragraph asserts that security drops below the category and decreases with every additional signature. Use the intended loss-of-guarantee wording while retaining the normative 2^24 limit. Same issue in the Introduction at lines 143–145.

The unescaped asterisks are parsed as Markdown emphasis, so the rendered draft loses the wildcard markers from this OID shorthand. Use inline code for the pattern here and at lines 269–271, 281, and 285 so the X.509 requirements retain their intended scope.
Added a workflow step to restore the editor team’s wildcard rule after generated files are updated. Commit: `5523135`.

comments.body: Yes, I agree. Can you remove that stuff?

Maybe so?

"Unlike the parameter sets of {{FIPS205}}, an SLH-DSA-FEW parameter set limits a single signing key to 2^24 signatures, a number that can be reached in practice (see {{sec-cons}}). Some generic measures to stay within the limit are:"
Agreed, can you rewrite it? I think the point is that here you do not need a counter at all, but some calculus beforehand and regular key updates, and you are fine.
See above :-)

I agree with Kaveh’s comment (R308 to R312). My goal with this suggestion is to make clear that the listed measures only apply to use cases where the signing limit could actually be exceeded, and that they are suggestions for preventing this, not requirements. I would suggest deleting lines R325 to R328.

```suggestion
Unlike the parameter sets of {{FIPS205}}, an SLH-DSA-FEW parameter set limits a single signing key to 2^24 signatures (see {{sec-cons}}). This limit can be reached in some realistic use cases; for example, a key that produces one signature per second reaches it in about 194 days. Where a use case could reach this limit, operators need to ensure that it is never exceeded. The following measures are suggestions for achieving this:
```

Could you elaborate on that? Do you mean that, instead of counting signatures, we should recommend determining the maximum aggregate signing rate across all instances holding the key (including HSMs, backups, and replicas), choosing a key lifetime so that this rate multiplied by the lifetime stays well below 2^24, and enforcing that rate for instance by rate-limiting the signing service?

Yes, you argue why you think that during the lifetime of the signer you will not pass the limit. This is part of NIST SP 800-230 (https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-230.ipd), so we might as well just point to it. See Section 3 in there:

> Because the security of these parameters depends entirely on adhering to this limit, users must perform a rigorous and complete evaluation of the operational environment for each signing key. This assessment should account for several critical factors, including the number of physical or virtual devices that share the same signing key, the maximum potential speed of each signing operation, the projected frequency of signature generation across all devices, and the total anticipated operational lifespan of the key. If an application’s requirements or operational controls cannot guarantee that the 224 signature limit will be respected, the parameter sets specified in this document must not be used.
